text: ResStock 2025 Release 1 Measure Documentation: HVAC Load Flexibility Accessing Results This documentation covers the “HVAC Load Flexibility” measure upgrade methodology and briefly discusses key results. All results can be accessed on the ResStock™ Open Energy Data Initiative “End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock” data lake and on the Data Viewer at resstock.nlr.gov. Measure Summary Measure Title HVAC Load Flexibility Measure Definition This upgrade lowers the heating set point and increases the cooling set point during predefined on-peak hours. It can also preheat or precool the dwelling units for 1 to 4 hours, depending on the measure settings. Applicability This measure applies to all dwellings with either a heating system or a cooling system that is approximately 99.7% of the building stock. Not Applicable This measure does not apply to the dwelling units that have neither a heating system nor a cooling system—approximately 0.3% of the building stock. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that the share of U.S. power generation from renewables will increase from 21% in 2021 to 44% in 2050 (EIA, 2022). This projected increase consists mainly of new wind and solar power, but wind and solar power are inherently variable energy sources, which poses a challenge for grid stability and control compared to fossil fuel- based power generation. For instance, solar power generation fluctuates with the time of day and weather, whereas wind energy is influenced by seasonal and atmospheric conditions. These fluctuations require sophisticated grid management to ensure a stable electricity supply. Flexible loads help balance supply and demand, especially as renewable energy increases. Many utility companies operate demand response programs. These programs range from interruptible service programs targeting large commercial and industrial customers, to rebates given to large customers for voluntary peak hour load reductions, to direct control of water heaters and air- conditioning compressors (Ryan Hledik A. R., 2022). Utilities such as Duke Energy (2024a), Xcel Energy (2024), and Pacific Gas and Electric Company (2024) enable demand response through time-based pricing where electricity rates vary by the time of day. By charging higher rates during peak hours and lower rates at other times, customers are encouraged to shift their usage to off-peak hours. Residential buildings account for a substantial share of U.S. electricity demand, representing 38% of the total electricity consumption in 2023 (EIA, 2024), making this sector the largest of all sectors. Demand flexibility within the residential building stock is crucial to achieving demand- side load flexibility, which can help balance grid loads. Within the residential sector, most load flexibility potential is found within the heating and cooling end uses because of the inherent thermal energy storage capability of the building’s heated or cooled mass.
